question: What happens in the heart that directly creates the pulse wave you feel in an artery?
explanation: When your left ventricle squeezes, it forces blood out into the aorta with great force. This creates a pressure wave that travels all the way down your arteries—and that's the pulse you feel! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T8#GNS111_U2_T8_h1)

question: Why do nurses check a patient's pulse during routine physical checks?

options.A: To calculate the total white blood cell production rate
options.B: To determine the precise volume of total body water
options.C: To measure the exact thickness of arterial muscle walls
options.D: To evaluate cardiovascular performance and tissue perfusion

explanation: Checking a pulse is a fast, easy way to see how well the heart is pumping blood and getting oxygen out to the rest of the body. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T8#GNS111_U2_T8_h1)

question: What do we call the natural ability of blood vessels to stretch and bounce back?
explanation: Compliance just means flexibility! It lets arteries stretch when the pulse wave rushes through and then recoil to keep pushing the blood forward. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T8#GNS111_U2_T8_h2)

question: How does stiffening of the arteries affect the pulse wave in older adults?

options.A: It doubles the total stroke volume of the heart
options.B: It slows down the heart rate to dangerous levels
options.C: It makes the pulse completely impossible to feel
options.D: It creates a bounding, high-amplitude pulse wave

explanation: When arteries lose their stretchiness and get stiff, they can't cushion the pressure wave. This makes the pulse feel much stronger or harder—often called a bounding pulse. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T8#GNS111_U2_T8_h2)

question: Which pulse site is standard to check during a routine check-up on an adult?
explanation: The radial pulse at the wrist is right near the surface and easy to reach, making it the go-to spot for routine checks. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T8#GNS111_U2_T8_h3)

question: A nurse wants to check blood flow to the foot of a patient with a suspected blocked leg artery. Which pulse should she check?
explanation: You'll find the dorsalis pedis right on top of the foot. It's the best spot to check if blood is successfully making it all the way down to the toes! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T8#GNS111_U2_T8_h3)

question: What usually happens to a patient's pulse rate if they experience sudden, heavy blood loss?

options.A: Complete disappearance of all peripheral pulses
options.B: No change in rate, only a drop in temperature
options.C: Severe bradycardia due to vagal nerve stimulation
options.D: Reflex tachycardia to maintain tissue perfusion

explanation: When blood volume drops, blood pressure falls. To make sure organs still get oxygen, the body quickens the heart rate (tachycardia) to keep things moving. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T8#GNS111_U2_T8_h4)

question: Why does a high fever usually cause a faster pulse rate?

options.A: The body has an increased metabolic demand
options.B: Fever directly destroys red blood cells
options.C: Heat slows down electrical signals in the brain
options.D: Elevated temperature freezes the heart valves

explanation: When you have a fever, your body's engine runs faster (higher metabolism). Because your cells need more oxygen and energy, your heart has to pump faster to keep up. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T8#GNS111_U2_T8_h4)

question: Why should a nurse avoid using their own thumb when checking a patient's pulse?

options.A: The thumb contains a distinct pulse that can be mistaken for the patient's
options.B: The thumb is too insensitive to feel any arterial movement
options.C: The thumb is anatomically incapable of pressing hard enough
options.D: Using the thumb violates standard hospital infection control rules

explanation: Your thumb has its own strong pulse running through it! If you use it to check a patient, you might end up counting your own heartbeat instead of theirs. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T8#GNS111_U2_T8_h5)

question: You notice a patient's heart rhythm is irregular during a routine check. How long should you count their pulse?
explanation: When a rhythm is irregular, a quick 30-second count won't give you an accurate picture. Counting for a full 60 seconds ensures you catch all those skipped beats and variations. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T8#GNS111_U2_T8_h5)

question: What is the normal resting pulse rate range for a healthy adult?
explanation: Commit this classic vital sign range to memory: a healthy adult at rest usually beats between 60 and 100 times per minute. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T8#GNS111_U2_T8_h6)

question: What does pulse 'volume' refer to when you are assessing a patient?

options.A: The exact speed of blood flow through veins
options.B: The total volume of blood in the entire body
options.C: The strength or amplitude of the pulse wave
options.D: The number of heart beats counted per minute

explanation: In nursing, pulse volume isn't about loudness or amount of blood—it's about how strong or weak (bounding or thready) the pulse feels under your fingers. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T8#GNS111_U2_T8_h6)

question: What do we call a resting adult heart rate that drops below 60 beats per minute?
explanation: Think of 'Brady' as slow (like bradycardia). When the heart rate dips below 60 bpm at rest, it's called bradycardia. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T8#GNS111_U2_T8_h7)

question: What does a 'pulse deficit' mean when a nurse compares an apical pulse to a radial pulse?

options.A: The patient has two different hearts beating at once
options.B: Some heart contractions fail to produce a palpable peripheral pulse
options.C: The radial artery is larger than the left ventricle
options.D: Blood pressure is too high for the peripheral vessels

explanation: A pulse deficit happens when the heart squeezes, but the beat is too weak to travel all the way to the wrist. So, if you listen at the chest (apical) you'll count more beats than you feel at the wrist (radial)! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T8#GNS111_U2_T8_h7)
